cues.text: Chapter six: Measuring experience and adoption.
Let us begin with a simple question.
When an organisation introduces a new digital service, how does it know whether the service is actually working for people?
Launching a system is not the same as succeeding with it.

To find out, we need measures, and this chapter walks through the most important ones, starting with how customers feel, then moving to whether they stay, and finally to whether they really use what we built.
The first measure is CSAT, which stands for Customer Satisfaction Score.
It is calculated as satisfied responses divided by valid responses, multiplied by one hundred percent.
Notice the word valid.
We only count responses that are usable, and we ask how many of those people were satisfied.
Take an example.
If eighty of one hundred respondents are satisfied, then CSAT equals eighty divided by one hundred, times one hundred, which is eighty percent.
So CSAT is eighty percent.
The second measure is the Net Promoter Score, or NPS.
Here customers are asked to give a rating, and the ratings are sorted into three groups.
Promoters are those who give a rating of nine or ten.
Detractors are those who give a rating from zero to six.
Passives are those who give seven or eight.
The formula is the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors.
Now, the passives are an interesting case.

They are included in the denominator, meaning they count among all the people surveyed when percentages are worked out, but they are not part of the numerator, so they add nothing to the score on either side.
Consider the example.
If sixty percent of respondents are promoters and twenty percent are detractors, then NPS equals sixty minus twenty, which is forty.
Because it is a difference between two percentages, NPS runs on a scale from minus one hundred to plus one hundred.
A score of minus one hundred would mean every respondent is a detractor, and plus one hundred would mean every respondent is a promoter.
The third measure is the Customer Effort Score.
It captures perceived effort, that is, how much work the customer felt they had to do to get something done.
The key caution here is that you must define the scale before you compare results.
If one team uses a one to five scale and another uses one to seven, or if the direction of the scale differs, then comparing their numbers would be misleading.
So agree the scale first, and only then compare.
Now we move from feelings to behaviour.
The next measure is retention.
Retention equals the customers from the starting cohort who are still active at the end, divided by the starting cohort, multiplied by one hundred percent.
A cohort is simply a group of customers who start together at the same point in time, and we follow that group.
Take the example.
If eight hundred of one thousand customers remain, retention is eight hundred divided by one thousand, times one hundred, which is eighty percent.
The flip side is churn, which is the share of customers lost.
For that cohort, churn is twenty percent.
Retention and churn together account for the whole starting group.
Next, adoption.
Adoption measures actual relevant use, not merely installed apps.
This is a vital distinction.
An app sitting on a phone, downloaded and never opened, is not adoption.
What counts is whether people use the service in the way that is relevant to its purpose.
Alongside these, the source tells us to also track several further measures.
Task completion, which is whether users manage to finish what they came to do.
First-contact resolution, which is whether their issue is solved the first time they reach out, without needing to come back.
Response time, which is how quickly the organisation replies.
Abandonment, which is how often users give up partway through.
And customer complaints, which show directly where the experience is failing.
Two practices make these numbers more trustworthy.
First, segment by channel and user group.
That means break the results down, for instance by app, website or phone line, and by different kinds of users, because an average can hide a group that is struggling.
Second, compare baseline and guardrail measures.
A baseline is where you started before the change, so you can see whether things really improved.
A guardrail measure is one you watch to make sure that improving one thing does not quietly damage another.
That leads to the closing example.
A support chatbot may reduce cost but increase unresolved complaints if it cannot hand off complex cases.
In other words, the bot may look efficient because it handles many conversations cheaply, yet customers with difficult problems get stuck, with no way to reach a human.
This is why we should evaluate completion and customer satisfaction, and not just bot interaction counts.
A high number of interactions says the bot was busy, not that it was helpful.
The final lesson of the chapter is this: human-centred measurement links process outcomes to business goals.

We measure from the customer's point of view, such as satisfaction, effort, completion and retention, and we connect those results to what the business is trying to achieve, so that digital efforts are judged by real value to people and to the organisation.
